title: Engineering a city-scale parcel-mapping practice
subtitle: How a core team of about ten delivered 1.5 million+ attributed land parcels across 35–40 cities on five continents, and the delivery system, automation and planning model that made it repeatable.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Core team of ~10; 20+ hired and trained

chapters.label: Brief
chapters.heading: Every parcel, every city, one standard
chapters.body:
The client, a global metaverse real-estate platform, needed real cities as plot-level land parcels. Each parcel had to be a clean polygon with an address and attributes, delivered as GeoJSON and ready to load straight into their platform.

The cities spanned Europe, the Americas, Australia, the Middle East and East Asia, and no two had the same starting point. Some had open cadastral data, some had usable OpenStreetMap coverage, and some had nothing but imagery. The delivery standard stayed fixed regardless: no overlaps or slivers, addresses matched to the right parcel, and attributes formatted exactly to the client's specification.

*The client is not named here, and every map and number in the interactive parts of this page is fictional.*

chapters.label: Constraint
chapters.heading: One on-ground lead
chapters.body:
The consultancy was small. The founding partner set the direction from the Netherlands, and the work on the ground in India ran through me: production, systems, hiring, training and the weekly client relationship.

That shaped every decision that followed. **The system had to work without me checking every parcel.** Quality had to be built into the process through stage procedures, QA gates and automated checks, not added at the end by one person.

chapters.label: System
chapters.heading: A 10-stage delivery framework
chapters.body:
I designed the framework, and refined it over four years, as ten stages in four phases. Every stage had a written **Workflow Procedure**, a step-by-step guide that let a new team member produce consistent work within days. QA gates sat at two levels: each **neighbourhood** was checked before moving on, and each **city** was checked before delivery. Every city started with a **preparation protocol** (source audit, client spec, edge cases) and ended with a **retrospective** that fed back into the procedures.

Parcels came from three routes, chosen city by city: digitising in QGIS over imagery where nothing usable existed, cleaning and restructuring open cadastral or OSM data where it did, and scripted processing on top of both.

chapters.label: Automation
chapters.heading: A script layer around the GIS work
chapters.body:
Repetitive, rule-based work moved into scripts integrated with the GIS workflow. These scripts handled:

- **Checking**: geometry validity, overlaps, gaps and missing attributes, before a human looked.
- **Extracting and retrieving**: pulling data out of layers and source files, and calling external APIs (Google Geocoding and Places, in batches).
- **Cleaning and integration**: parsing responses, standardising address components to each city's local conventions, and merging results back onto parcels.
- **Formatting and QA**: shaping output to the client's schema and checking it against the delivery criteria automatically.

The clearest gain was **address extraction**, the 0.25 h benchmark you'll see in the planner below. Done manually, it took about 1.5 hours per 1,000 parcels. The automated pipeline batch-called the API, parsed and cleaned the response, and flagged only the exceptions (missing numbers, ambiguous matches, addresses falling outside the parcel) for a person to review. That brought it down to about **0.25 hours per 1,000 parcels, an 83% reduction**. Across the 1M+ parcels processed after deployment, that works out to roughly **1,250 person-hours saved**.

note.title: How the 1,250 hours is derived
note.body: (1.5 h − 0.25 h) per 1,000 parcels × ~1,000,000 parcels after deployment ≈ 1,250 hours. It's an estimate from the measured per-1,000 rates, not a logged total.

chapters.label: Planning
chapters.heading: A capacity & deadline model that held its dates
chapters.body:
Committing to a city delivery date with a small team means accounting for everything that eats capacity. I built a capacity and deadline model, with AI help on the formula logic, that turns a city's scope into a dated plan. It has four sections:

1. **Scope:** the target parcel count, plus status counts pulled from ClickUp (mapped, spatially cleaned, final-cleaned), so the model can re-plan a city that is already in progress. Each of the ten stages has a **benchmark in hours per 1,000 parcels**, and stage hours roll up into four groups: MP→AM, SC→SP, FC and global final review. City-prep tasks (preparation, pricing and landmarks, boundary cleaning per neighbourhood, pilot neighbourhoods) are checked against prep capacity.
2. **Team capacity:** each person's hours per day and days per week, with part of the week allocated to final clean.
3. **Rules:** structured deductions typed as **Must** (unavoidable: admin, management, onboarding ramp-up, holidays) or **Buffer** (conservative: unplanned leave, side projects). Each applies to mapping, final clean or both, for a person or the whole team, in hours per day, week or month, within an optional week window.
4. **Weekly summary:** two scenarios, **S1** (gross minus Must) and **S2** (also minus Buffer), run week by week to give dated milestones. S2 is the date committed to.

In use, its finish dates held at about **95% accuracy** against actual completion, including the unexpected leave and extra work that always turn up.

chapters.label: Operations
chapters.heading: Running parallel cities with a small team
chapters.body:
Several cities ran at once through ClickUp: each **city is a project**, each **stage is a list** with its own checklist, and **dashboards with time tracking** showed where every neighbourhood stood and who was working on it. I used it together with the timeline model to drive all workload allocation and delivery planning.

I also owned the people side end to end: sourcing, a technical screen, an **assignment-based evaluation** (candidates did a real mapping task) and around 100 interviews, then onboarding, training and performance reviews. Over four years that came to 20+ people, with a core team of about 10 at any time.

And I wrote the documentation that held it together: workflow processes, technology, administrative and hiring processes, and **user manuals for every automation and tool** we built.

chapters.label: Client & growth
chapters.heading: Owning the relationship
chapters.body:
For more than three years I was the client's primary contact, sending weekly progress and strategy reports and handling scope questions city by city. I drafted the pre-final **client–consultant service agreement** from scratch, legal terms included.

On growth, I led outreach to **Dutch municipalities**, **Indian government tenders** and **freelance platforms**, backed by city-level desk research and stakeholder interviews to test where the practice could expand.

chapters.label: Outcomes
chapters.heading: What it added up to
chapters.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| Cities delivered | 35–40, across 5 continents |
| Parcels | 1.5M+ individually attributed polygons |
| Address processing | −83% time per 1,000 parcels |
| Hours saved (est.) | ~1,250 across 1M+ parcels |
| Planning accuracy | ~95% on finish dates |
| Team | 20+ hired and trained over four years; core team of ~10 |
| Client relationship | 3+ years as primary liaison |

chapters.label: Reflection
chapters.heading: What I'd build next
chapters.body:
Everything above is **rule-based**: procedures, scripts and checks I wrote by hand. It scaled, but each new city still needed people to digitise, and each new edge case needed a new rule.

The next step is to let models take on part of that work:

- **Parcel extraction from imagery** with segmentation models, with people correcting the output rather than drawing from scratch.
- **Learned match confidence** for addresses, so review effort goes only where the model is unsure.
- **Anomaly detection in QA**, flagging parcels that look statistically unlike their neighbours.

That's the gap I want to close with formal training in spatial data science and GeoAI.
